Drops November 6th. Pre-sale October 30th. Everywhere.

Jesus is THE reason for the season.

That’s the whole thesis, and it’s the reason I recorded this EP. Emmanuel is three tracks, out now, built for people who want their Christmas music to remember who Christmas is about.

Emmanuel means “God with us.” Everything else in December is decoration. The lights, the food, the gifts, the tree: all good, all downstream. This EP points back upstream. 

The tracks

1. Emmanuel — Y2K bubblegum pop at a mid-tempo bounce. It’s bright and sweet, and it sounds like the glossy pop of your childhood. The song is a doorway. It sounds like candy and carries the oldest news there is.

2. This Christmas — A synthpop shuffle at a slinky 126 BPM. It’s a prayer set to a groove: that Christmas wouldn’t end on December 26th, and that real peace on Earth would last all year long. A simple chord progression, a mono synth bass line, a tapping foot. It’s light on its feet and built for kitchen dancing. It was brewed on the Olympic Peninsula, and it sits warm in the belly.

3. Jesus Is King — The quietest track on the EP, and the heart of it. Dialed-back, with a woolly synth bass, flute, sax, and a honey-drenched vocal. It’s where the party stops and the room goes still. If the first two tracks are the celebration, this one is the kneeling.

Why a Christmas EP, and why now

Most of the music made about Christmas has drifted away from Christmas itself. I wanted to add something to the season that doesn’t flinch. It should be fun, because joy is a fruit of the Spirit. It should be well made, because craft is a form of worship. And it should be unembarrassed about the name at the center.

I perform synthpop and vaporwave under Claim The Word, a music ministry out of rural Clallam County on the Olympic Peninsula. The sound is electronic, but the aim is old: claim the word, speak it, and let it go out.

Where to listen

  • Normie Outlets:
    • Spotify
    • YouTube Music
    • Apple Music
    • Amazon Music 
  • Direct-support Outlets:
    • Bandcamp
    • Subvert 
(If you want to support the work directly, direct-support outlets are the best places to do it. Both include significant bonus material you won’t find on the streaming platforms):

A few ways to help

If the EP lands with you, here’s what actually moves the needle for an independent artist:

  1. Add a track to your Christmas playlist. Playlist adds are the lifeblood of discovery.
  2. Share it with one person. A friend, a family member, a group chat.
  3. Play it at an actual gathering. Dinner, the tree-trimming, the drive to grandma’s. These songs were made for company.

What’s next

The Christmas season is a short window, so spend it well. Then in January the next chapter opens with The Body of Christ, set for January 29, 2027. It’s the first step in a longer arc, and I’ll share more soon.

One last thing

If you only press play on one track, make it This Christmas. If you press play on a second, make it Jesus Is King. And if you’re in a room with someone you love, turn it up and dance a little.

Merry Christmas. God with us, all year long.

Cloth Has No Power

Conscience, the Collective, and the Question Every Citizen Must Answer for him or herself.

I. The Gentle Answer and the Hard Question

Ask most people what a flag means and you will get a gentle answer. It stands for shared history. It says thank you for roads, courts, hospitals, and neighbors. It honors people who gave something real for the place we call home. Nothing in that answer is wrong.

Now ask a different question: What would you refuse to do if your flag asked?

Most of us have never been asked that. Many of us have never asked it of ourselves. Yet it is the only question that tells us what the flag means to us in practice. A flag is not dangerous because of what it is. It is dangerous because of what it can be used to request.

This essay is an invitation to everyone, believer and skeptic, veteran and conscientious objector, to think carefully about where loyalty ends and surrender begins. It is addressed especially to Christians, because we are the ones who claim a Lord above every nation, and so we are the ones with the least excuse for losing track of the line.

We write as a Christian ministry that holds to salvation by grace alone through faith alone, and we write as people who want to work shoulder to shoulder with neighbors of every belief to serve those in need. Those two commitments are not in tension. They are the reason this essay exists. We include ourselves in every question it asks.

II. What a Flag Is, and What It Is Not

A flag is dyed cloth on a pole. It has no will and no power. Anyone who fears it as though it carried a curse, or reveres it as though it carried a blessing, has wandered into superstition.

Paul addressed a nearly identical problem in Corinth. Believers there were anxious about meat offered to idols. His answer was calm: an idol is nothing at all in the world (1 Corinthians 8). The stone and wood had no power, and no one is condemned by eating the wrong meat.

But Paul did not stop there. He added that fellowship with what stands behind the idol is another matter, and that a believer must not sit at the table of demons (1 Corinthians 10). The object was nothing. The act of binding yourself to what the object represents was something.

Flags work the same way. The cloth is nothing. The question is what the cloth is being used to gather people into.

Loving one's home is a good thing. God places people in nations and in times (Acts 17:26). Jeremiah told exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city where they lived (Jeremiah 29:7). Gratitude for civic order, honor for the dead, and care for those who came home wounded are fitting expressions of love. None of that is the problem.

III. Where Idolatry Actually Lives

Scripture is consistent about where idolatry takes root, and it is almost never in the object.

In Isaiah 44, a craftsman cuts down a tree. With half the wood he warms himself and bakes bread. With the other half he carves a god and bows to it, saying, Deliver me, for you are my god. Isaiah's diagnosis is not that wood is dangerous. A deluded heart has led the man astray, and he cannot bring himself to ask, Is there not a lie in my right hand?

The lie is in the hand. The wood merely receives it.

Jesus says the same in Matthew 6, not about a statue but about a ledger: You cannot serve God and money. Wealth has no temple in that sentence. It has a master's claim on a servant's will. Paul in Romans 1 describes people who exchanged the truth about God for a lie and served created things instead of the Creator.

Idolatry, then, is not a category of objects. It is a direction of allegiance. Anything can occupy the seat: a statue, a fortune, a movement, a family, a party, a nation, even a church. The seat is the issue. Who gets the final yes?

So we state the principle plainly: idolatry begins when a good thing is given ultimate authority over conscience. This is why the thesis of this essay is not about fabric. Idolatry is never in the cloth. It is in the human will that surrenders its conscience to the collective.

 IV. The Golden Image and the Band

The book of Daniel contains what may be the most precise case study on this subject, and its sharpest detail is easy to miss.

Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden image on the plain of Dura. The order is simple: when you hear the horn, flute, lyre, and the full ensemble, fall down and worship, or be thrown into a furnace. The whole empire complies. Three Jewish administrators do not.

Look at what they say. They do not denounce the statue or lecture the king about metallurgy. They say they will not serve his gods or worship the image he has set up. Their refusal is aimed at compelled ultimate loyalty backed by the full force of the state.

Notice also the trigger. The crowd was not argued into bowing. It was cued, by music, spectacle, and the pressure of thousands of bodies dropping to their knees at once. Total loyalty rarely arrives as an argument. It arrives as a ceremony.

The point is not that every anthem is Nebuchadnezzar's band. The point is that the Bible understands exactly how this works, and it names the refusal that matters: not "I dislike this object," but "my conscience is not yours to command."

V. Whose Image Is on You?

Matthew 22 gives us the most quoted line on this subject, and it is usually read as if it settled the question in favor of easy compliance.

The religious leaders try to trap Jesus with a question about the imperial tax. He asks for a coin. Whose image and inscription is this? Caesar's. Then give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.

Read it slowly. The coin bears Caesar's image, so it goes back to Caesar. Now ask the second half: what bears God's image? Genesis 1:27 answers. Human beings do.

The sentence is not a tidy split of life into a civic half and a spiritual half. It is a quiet declaration that Caesar's claim is limited by a more fundamental claim, one stamped on the persons he governs. The state has a measured claim on coins. It has no claim at all on the conscience of the people made in God's image.

Jesus is not teaching resistance. He is teaching proportion. And proportion is exactly what is lost when a nation begins to speak in the language of ultimate things.

VI. A Pattern, Not an Accident

If this were only an ancient problem, we could leave it in Babylon. It is not.

Look across the last century and a pattern emerges that crosses every flag, party, and ideology. States ask ordinary people to give up things that should never be given up, and they ask in the language of belonging.

German soldiers in two world wars wore belt buckles stamped with the words God with us. Chaplains on opposing sides blessed the same kind of guns and prayed to the same God for opposite outcomes. In 1938, Protestant pastors in Germany were required to swear a personal oath of loyalty to Hitler. Many did. The Confessing Church had already written the Barmen Declaration in 1934, insisting that Christ alone holds the church's ultimate allegiance and that no other lord may claim it. Those who held to that confession paid heavily, and the best-known of them, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, was executed.

In the United States, pulpits defended slavery with Scripture, and other pulpits, reading the same Bible, called for its abolition. In 1942, roughly 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them American citizens, were forced from their homes and held in camps. Most of the country, including most churches, said little. In many places, majority-Christian communities have taken part in, or looked away from, the killing of their own neighbors when the collective demanded it.

We are not listing these to assign blame to any one nation or tradition. We are listing them because they share a shape. In each case, what the state asked for was not a flag salute. It was a moral sacrifice: to look away, to lie, to hate, to hand over a neighbor, to kill, to fund killing, to stay silent. And in each case, the request arrived wrapped in loyalty, belonging, and the sense that refusing was unthinkable.

Every state asks something. Not every state asks the same thing, and not every request is wrong. But the pattern is old enough and wide enough that no citizen of any country, in any era, should assume the question will never come. Nor should we assume that the current moment is the one safe exception.

VII. Paying, Serving, Consenting

Here is the center of the argument, and it needs care.

The commandment against murder is not suspended by a uniform. In the Christian moral tradition, taking human life is gravely serious, and the traditions that permit it do so only under tight conditions. The classical Just War framework, developed by Augustine and Aquinas, requires just cause, legitimate authority, right intention, last resort, proportionality, and a reasonable hope of success. Notice where it places the burden of proof: on the war, not on the conscience that doubts it. By its own logic, a Christian who cannot see those conditions met is not merely permitted but obligated to hesitate.

Other streams go further. Anabaptists, Mennonites, and Quakers have held for centuries that the way of Jesus excludes violence entirely, and many early Christian writers, such as Tertullian and Origen, shared the conviction. The Catholic Catechism teaches that citizens are obliged in conscience not to follow civil directives that contradict the moral order, and it calls for humane provision for conscientious objectors. The Nuremberg principles, adopted after the twentieth century's worst atrocities, rest on the same insight: "I was following orders" is no defense when a moral choice was possible.

What about taxes? We should be honest. Jesus affirmed giving to Caesar what is Caesar's, and Paul told Roman Christians to pay what they owed (Romans 13:6-7), under a government that would eventually execute him. Paying is not the sin.

The sin is consenting. There is a vast moral difference between a believer who pays under compulsion, grieves what is done with the money, and works to change it, and a believer who celebrates, recruits for, blesses, or falls silent about a cause they never examined. Faithful people land in different places along that spectrum: some pay and protest, some pay and work to change the law, some, like many Quakers, resist war taxes and accept the legal consequences. All are responding sincerely to a real tension. None should be shamed.

What no one should do is pretend the tension does not exist. The danger is the moment a person stops asking is this just? and starts asking only whose side are we on? That is where the flag quietly takes the seat of the judge. It is not the soldier who serves with a clear conscience, or the taxpayer who pays and prays, who has made an idol. It is the one who has handed the question itself to someone else.

VIII. Why Grace Alone Makes This Possible

We hold that we are saved by grace through faith alone, apart from works. This is not a side note to our argument. It is the reason the argument can be made at all.

Many Christians feel a quiet pressure to prove their standing through loyalty, as if declining a national ritual were a failure that God will count against them, or as if joining one were the proof that they are good. That is a works religion dressed in patriotic clothes. It says: prove your loyalty, perform the ritual, pay the price, show you belong. It runs on anxiety.

The gospel runs on rest. If our standing before God rests on Christ and not on our performance, then no national ritual can add to it or subtract from it. Standing for an anthem does not save anyone. Declining to recite a pledge does not condemn anyone. The person who is secure in Christ is free precisely because nothing the state demands can touch the one thing that matters.

That freedom cuts both ways. It frees us to serve, to give, to honor, and to love our country without fear. And it frees us, when conscience requires, to refuse without fear. Good works flow from salvation. They are never the price of it, and neither is obedience to a nation.

This is also why a Christian can afford to ask uncomfortable questions of the nation, and why the question is no betrayal. A person who needs the state's approval to feel secure cannot examine the state. A person who is already held by grace can.

IX. The Audit: Questions for the Conscience

An essay that only informs has failed. So here, plainly, is the invitation. These questions are for everyone. They are meant especially for Christians, who claim a Lord above every flag. We ask them of ourselves first.

About what has already been asked:

  • What has my country already asked its citizens to give up morally, and what did I give without asking whether it was right?
  • Where have I accepted a lie because the truth was inconvenient to my side?
  • Where have I looked away because the person being harmed was far away, or foreign, or not like me?
  • What have I paid for, praised, or defended in the name of the nation without ever examining it?

About what could be asked:

  • What is the one thing I would refuse to do even if my government, my church, my family, and my friends all demanded it?
  • If the answer is "nothing," what does that say about who holds my ultimate loyalty?
  • Would I recognize the moment it was asked of me, or has loyalty already trained me not to notice?

About how I stand with others:

  • Can I honor those who serve and still ask hard questions about those who sent them?
  • Can I respect a neighbor who lands differently than I do on war, taxes, or conscience, and still hold my own conviction?
  • Am I willing to stand beside people of other faiths and none, in service, without pretending we agree on everything?

For the Christian especially:

  • Is there any banner, in my heart or in my sanctuary, that competes with the cross?
  • When Scripture and the nation's story disagree, which one do I quietly edit?
  • Do I trust grace enough to risk my reputation, my comfort, or my standing in the tribe for the sake of conscience?

These are not rhetorical. Sit with them. Write your answers down. Revisit them in a year.

X. Common Ground, Honest Differences

We said this essay was meant to build bridges. Here is where the bridges already stand.

Anabaptists and Quakers will recognize the argument at once. They have lived it, and paid for it, for centuries.

Catholics and Orthodox Christians carry deep resources on conscience, just war, and the limits of state authority, and their saints and martyrs stand squarely in this tradition.

The Black church tradition has insisted for generations that a nation can praise liberty while practicing bondage, and that the gospel judges the flag, not the reverse. Frederick Douglass drew a sharp line between the Christianity of Christ and the "Christianity of this land." That is the line we are drawing.

Jewish neighbors know Daniel 3 as their own story, and rabbinic tradition has long treated idolatry as a matter of allegiance, not just objects.

Muslim neighbors will hear a close cousin of shirk, the setting up of partners alongside the One God, a category that was never only about statues.

Secular peace advocates, veterans, and humanitarian workers often share the conviction that conscience cannot be outsourced. Some of the strongest voices against careless war belong to people who have seen it up close.

We do not claim these traditions agree about God, salvation, or Scripture. They do not, and we are not interested in blurring the differences. But we can stand together on this: no state is god, and no person made in God's image is merely a tool of the collective. Where we stand together, we can act together: feeding the hungry, housing the displaced, sitting with the grieving, welcoming the stranger. We can educate one another honestly along the way, differences intact.

Because we hold that salvation is a gift, we are not there to earn anything or to win anyone. We are free to serve beside anyone who is serving, and free to learn from them.

XI. Objections Worth Taking Seriously

"Romans 13 says to submit to governing authorities." It does, and the passage deserves its full weight. But the same Paul was jailed by those authorities, and the apostles said they must obey God rather than men. Most of the Christian tradition reads Romans 13 as describing government's proper function, not granting it unlimited claim on conscience. Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, and Anabaptist readers differ on where the limits fall, but nearly all agree there are limits."Cornelius was a centurion, and the New Testament never tells him to quit." True, and many Christians conclude that soldiering can be an honorable vocation. It can be. Others note that the same silence leaves slaveholders unaddressed by name, yet no one concludes that slavery is fine. Silence invites wisdom, not a blank check.

"Just War theory exists so Christians can support some wars." It does, and we respect it. But it is a test, not a permission slip. A believer who applies it honestly will sometimes conclude a given war fails, and the tradition says that conclusion binds.

"A flag is just a symbol, and symbols are neutral." The cloth is neutral. But symbols are how communities remember, bind, and sometimes coerce. A thing powerless in itself can still carry a very powerful pressure, which is exactly what the golden image did.

"This disrespects people who served." It must not, and where it does, we have failed. Honoring those who served, mourning those who died, and caring for those who came home wounded are fully compatible with asking hard questions of the institutions that sent them. Often the people with the most authority to ask are the ones who paid for the answers.

"Doesn't this make politics a test of salvation?" No. That is the point of grace. No one is saved by the position they take on war, taxes, or flags. We are saved by Christ alone. What we are asking is how a saved person, who is free, uses that freedom.

XII. Closing

Nebuchadnezzar's furnace was heated seven times hotter than usual, and the three who refused went in without a defense, a plan, or a guarantee. What they said before they went is the sentence the church keeps needing to hear: Our God is able to deliver us. But even if he does not, we will not bow.

Cloth cannot save us, and it cannot condemn us. The question was never about the fabric. It is about who gets the final yes, and what we will say when the request comes, as it comes to every generation.

So love your country. Thank your neighbors. Honor your dead. And keep one word in reserve, the word that belongs to God alone. Then ask yourself, honestly, what that word has already cost you, and what you have already given away without noticing.

Psychodrama, Liminality, and the Collapse of Interior Space

Walllpaper.com, The New York Times, Psychology Today — countless outlets reviewing Backrooms reach for the same word: liminal. Everyone calls it a movie about liminal spaces. And of course it's true. But it's an oversimplification. The film's real achievement isn't that it embraces the liminal aesthetic, its inherent anxieties, its reality. Rather, the film subtly relocates liminality. Assuming the phenomenon is real, Backrooms is quietly asking a harder question than the reviews give it credit for: where, exactly, is liminal space? Where does the phenomenon actually occur?

That question matters more than it looks, because this is not a small movie asking it. Backrooms is a polarizing, high-concept horror film that outperforms legacy IPs by leaning into original, internet-born mythology rather than franchise continuity. In its opening weekend it out-drew a $165 million Star Wars spinoff while costing roughly $10 million to make, and went on to become A24's highest-grossing release ever, crossing $330 million worldwide.1 It resonates most strongly with Millennial and Gen Z/Alpha audiences — nearly 85 percent of opening-weekend crowds were under 35 — as a return to form: adventurous, experimental storytelling rooted in a shared cultural sense that originality has been in decline since roughly the early 2010s.2 For others it may register as shallow or overly stylized, contentless aesthetic dressed as meaning — meme logic masquerading as cinema, generational noise to anyone outside the audience that had already spent years building the film's mythology on Reddit and fan wikis before A24 ever got involved.3

That dismissal misses the argument the film is actually making.

Where liminality used to live

For years, internet culture imagined liminality as something external. Empty shopping malls. Endless hotel hallways. Abandoned schools. Office buildings after midnight. Spaces that felt strangely familiar yet completely devoid of purpose — as though reality, like a computer program, had been left running long after everyone moved on, had gone home, logged off for good. The scene exploded via Tumblr around 2010, riding a fascination with late-twentieth-century nostalgia, vaporwave, and VR lobby original-soundtrack aesthetics (today's elevator music), and it eventually curdled into the Backrooms mythos itself — which, notably, began as an anonymous 2019 creepypasta and metastasized across Reddit, fan wikis, and fan-made games for years before any studio touched it. 

A 20-year-old filmmaker inherited that collectively authored folklore; he didn't invent it.4 After years of that organic build-up, Backrooms captured a peculiar feeling that millions of people already recognized and had been trying to describe. There was always something deeper underneath it.

The liminal aesthetic has always reminded me of an almost Newtonian view of reality — in the scientific sense, but philosophically too. Reality feels like a continuous stream only because we're moving through it moment by moment in a way that merely seems seamless. But are moments simply momenting? Imagine time experienced as discrete frames, rendered one after another. What if someone slipped behind those frames? The moments would become places. And places left behind wouldn't necessarily be haunted — they'd be worse than haunted. 

Vacant.

Isolated. Without a spark of connection: airports without travelers, restaurants without customers, beer without effervescence, matches that refuse to ignite. Time moves on and leaves behind a void repulsed by its own uncanny silence.

That's the logic underneath Stephen King's The Langoliers, often considered a proto-liminal masterpiece — which is why the TV movie adaptation still feels remarkably modern. Long before "liminal space" entered internet vocabulary, King imagined yesterday itself as a discarded world, a forgotten moment-place. If The Langoliers imagined the liminality of time, and the internet imagined the liminality of place, then Backrooms does something very different, almost as sleight of hand: it doesn't reject or redefine liminality. Backrooms pinpoints Liminality's origin and reassigns its real location. It gives proper astral coordinates to a moment-place that was supposed to be a myth — and locates liminality, instead, in the mind.

The Catalyst

At its center, Backrooms is built around two figures: Clark, a failed architect turned furniture-store owner (Chiwetel Ejiofor), and Mary, his therapist (Renate Reinsve).5 The film is nearly split in half — an A/B test of a theme park, start against end — pivoting on how the handler copes with a world authored by her patient. Psychodrama isn't a passing detail here. It's the engine. It's the catalyst — the scene in Mary's office, roughly twenty minutes in, right where a catalyst belongs structurally, that sets the entire plot in motion. What begins as therapeutic reenactment doesn't stay contained. It becomes generative. Trauma is staged, repeated, re-entered, and in the repetition it starts to mutate. The film asks an unsettling question: what happens when reenactment becomes recursive? What happens when the search for healing generates another layer of the labyrinth — when the process meant to organize suffering starts reproducing it instead?

From there the film's logic changes. The psychodrama stops merely interpreting experience and starts producing environment. The Backrooms emerge as a recursive extension of reenacted trauma — memory rendered spatial, interiority rendered architectural — degrading with each iteration until the mind becomes a maze: an ever-scaling nightmare of identical yellow corridors. Each attempt to understand the past generates another hallway. The reenactment of trauma doesn't merely occur inside the Backrooms — it's the mechanism by which the Backrooms come into being. Therapy isn't a path through the maze. It's the process that generates the maze.

That's the film's most fascinating move: the never-ending hallway isn't a symptom of anything. It isn't a disease. It's a poke at a hornet's nest. The real horror here isn't a spooky building. It's a consciousness that has become unscalable architecture. By constant questioning, relentless recursion, abandoned echoes, the Backrooms stop being simply a place someone wanders into — they become the spatial expression of recursive thought, a mind so consumed with processing itself that it eventually starts constructing the very maze it hopes to escape. That transforms the entire tradition of liminality. And whether Kane Parsons and his team intended this direction or not, the concept-shift raises enormous questions about modern therapeutic culture. One critic put it in psychoanalytic terms — that the unconscious here isn't something we merely have, but something that inhabits us and can ultimately destroy us.6

Putting the Establishment on Trial

Those questions are bigger than horror. They're questions about human nature, and about the institutions built to manage it. The film puts modern psychotherapy — and even the monotony of self-help culture — on trial. Loud and clear, on the big screen: a criticism of medical-establishment deep-capture, the sort of institution-backed do-gooding that unwittingly imposes darkness onto the hurting and the vulnerable.

And I want to push on this rather than just note it: today mental health is treated as an ivory box. Good for you, but don't you dare open it up and look inside — and God forbid you scrutinize the establishment itself. Take the pills. Do the psychodrama, or you get marked "difficult to assist." That posture is a real problem, and Backrooms puts the topic front and center in a way that feels less like accident and more like the one thing the director didn't want the audience to miss. None of this means the whole apparatus is worthless. People have genuinely been helped by all kinds of dangerous things throughout history, and even a broken clock is right twice a day. But right twice a day isn't a foundation.

The Older Truth

From where I stand as a Christian, this is where Backrooms unexpectedly brushes against something much older than internet folklore or modern psychotherapy. Christianity teaches that man cannot, ultimately, redeem himself. Follow that principle to its conclusion and a maze built entirely from recursive self-engagement contains no exit by design. If the self is both the wound and the physician, every answer eventually curves back toward the same center. Things get ugly. The rooms multiply rather than diminish. The architect — his brokenness — isn't trapped so much as encapsulated within a vapor blueprint: never happened, never will, always has.

The question the film keeps circling is whether the self can ultimately rescue the self. Christianity answers that with a decisive no — not because self-examination has no value, but because redemption comes from outside the maze, from a reality the maze cannot generate on its own. This isn't an argument against examining ourselves; scripture repeatedly calls us to do exactly that. Repent every day. But repentance and recursive self-therapy are not the same motion. One looks outward for the thing that can actually redeem. The other just keeps rearranging the furniture around an open wound, on the theory that a better floor plan is the same thing as healing.

That, to me, is what makes Backrooms linger long after the credits roll. It doesn't simply ask whether liminal spaces exist. It asserts where they exist. And its answer is profoundly unsettling: not in abandoned malls, not in forgotten office buildings, not somewhere behind reality — but in the human mind itself. Left to orbit itself long enough, consciousness doesn't just get lost. Encouraged to relive itself endlessly, the mind prefers dementia. It becomes impossible. And its architecture becomes a reflection of reality — the only kind of reflection recursive self-engagement was ever capable of producing.

 

 FOOTNOTES:

  1. A24's Backrooms, directed by Kane Parsons and produced for about $10 million, had grossed more than $330 million worldwide as of late June 2026, making it the highest-grossing film in the studio's history and beating a $165 million Star Wars spinoff at the box office in its release weekend. Deadline, "How 'Backrooms' Blew Doors Off Box Office With $118M WW Opening," May 2026; Variety, "Box Office: 'Backrooms' Stuns...," May 31, 2026.

  2. PostTrak data cited by Variety showed roughly 85 percent of opening-weekend audiences under age 35, with more than half 25 or younger — figures echoed by Deadline's Screen Engine/Rentrak exit data. Variety, "'Backrooms' Box Office: Kane Parsons' Horror Success Explained," June 2, 2026.

  3. Deadline reported that A24 built its marketing around communities on YouTube, TikTok, and Reddit who had already spent years developing the Backrooms mythology and lore before the studio got involved. Deadline, May 2026.

  4. The Backrooms originated as an anonymous 2019 4chan creepypasta and spread through Reddit, fan wikis, and fan-made games for years before Kane Parsons' web series and the eventual A24 feature. Deadline, May 2026.

  5. Character and cast details — Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor) and Mary (Renate Reinsve) — and director/writer credits (Kane Parsons, directing; Will Soodik, screenplay, from an earlier draft by Roberto Patino) per Wikipedia, "Backrooms (film)," and IMDb.

  6. Ira Israel, "'Backrooms': Film Review," Psychology Today, June 2026 — reads the film's unconscious as something that inhabits and can destroy the self, rather than something merely possessed.

A Morning Meditation from Matthew 5–7 (KJV)

Some mornings begin with birdsong. Others begin with lists.

We’ve all been there. You’re lying in bed, staring at the ceiling instead of sleeping. Maybe tomorrow has already arrived in your mind. Projects. Conversations. Bills. Regrets. Things you wish you’d said differently. Things you wish you’d done sooner.

So you get up and make a list. Lists are comforting. They organize the chaos. They quiet the mind—at least for a little while.

That was me recently.

I’ve always been an action-oriented person. I enjoy building things, writing music, solving problems, serving people. Sometimes that becomes its own temptation. I want to do. If I’m not careful, I begin believing that every quiet moment is wasted.

Yet God occasionally stops even the busiest hands at a red light.

That night, after my lists were finished and sleep still refused to come, there wasn’t much left to accomplish except thank the Lord Jesus Christ for His guidance and trust His timing.

Eventually, sleep came—not because I’d solved everything, but because He never asked me to.

The next morning I reached for my Bible before I reached for the news. Not because the news doesn’t matter. Because perspective matters more.

For reasons I can’t entirely explain, I opened Matthew. Sometimes the Holy Ghost nudges us gently. I’ve learned not to argue.

The Family Resemblance

The Beatitudes have always fascinated me.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
“Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.” (Matthew 5:3,5 KJV)

Notice how each blessing carries its own promise. Some inherit the Kingdom. Some inherit the earth. Some obtain mercy. Some are called the children of God.

As I read, I couldn’t help but wonder if Jesus is giving us a glimpse of something wonderfully intricate about His coming Kingdom. Salvation itself is gloriously simple—we are saved by grace through faith in Christ alone—but perhaps, once safely home, the virtues cultivated during this life become part of how God delights to order His eternal Kingdom.

That isn’t something I would insist upon as doctrine. It’s simply an observation that makes me marvel at how carefully Jesus chose every word.

Either way, one thing becomes unmistakably clear. These aren’t merely behaviors. They’re family traits. They’re the sort of heart the Holy Spirit grows inside those who belong to Christ.

Jesus Raises the Standard

As Matthew continues, something remarkable happens. Jesus doesn’t lower God’s expectations. He raises them beyond anything mankind could ever accomplish.

It’s no longer merely, “Thou shalt not kill.” Now anger itself matters. It’s no longer merely avoiding adultery. Even lust is brought into the light (Matthew 5:21–28).

At first glance, this almost feels discouraging. Until we realize what Jesus is doing. He’s exposing the impossible. The Pharisees had become experts at polishing the outside while neglecting the inside.

Jesus quietly dismantles that entire system.

God has always seen the heart. The anger. The pride. The envy. The bitterness. The hidden conversations nobody else hears. Suddenly it becomes obvious that none of us can stand before a perfectly holy God on our own record.

That realization isn’t meant to crush us. It’s meant to point us to the only One who never failed. Jesus fulfilled what none of us could.

The Debt We Could Never Pay

That thought stayed with me as I continued reading. Our culture loves the language of “paying people back.” Get even. Settle the score. Make them answer. Jesus points in another direction. Why? Because every believer knows something deeply personal.

We were carrying a debt we could never satisfy ourselves. Christ satisfied it.

The cross wasn’t a partial payment. It wasn’t a down payment. It was enough.

When I remember how much I’ve been forgiven, it becomes harder to keep a ledger against everyone else.

Jesus later teaches,

“For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matthew 6:14 KJV)

Forgiveness doesn’t pretend evil never happened. It simply refuses to become chained to it.

Quiet Faith Is Strong Faith

One theme keeps surfacing throughout these chapters. Don’t perform righteousness. Live it. When you pray, pray. When you give, give. When you fast, don’t advertise your suffering.

Jesus says,

“But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face.” (Matthew 6:17 KJV)

There’s something wonderfully freeing about that. Our Father sees what nobody else sees. The applause of strangers fades almost immediately. The approval of God does not.

Looking Through Christ Instead of Guilt

As I closed my Bible, one phrase stayed with me. Sometimes we spend our entire day looking through what I’d call a guilt prism. Everything passes through it. Yesterday’s failures. Today’s shortcomings. Tomorrow’s worries. Eventually we begin believing that this distorted picture is reality.

Christ hands us a different lens. Not one that excuses sin. One that properly explains it. Yes, I have failed. Yes, I still stumble. But Jesus Christ has already satisfied the debt that stood against me. 

That changes everything.

Instead of asking, “How can I earn God’s acceptance today?” I can ask, “Lord, because You have already accepted me in Christ, how can I reflect You today?”

That’s a completely different way to wake up.

Walking the Narrow Way

Jesus ends these teachings with the image of two gates. One broad. One narrow. The broad way invites us to trust ourselves. To become self-righteous. To judge others while quietly excusing our own hearts. The narrow gate asks something much harder.

Trust Christ instead.

That path often feels lonely. Sometimes you’ll feel like you’re swimming upstream while the world rushes confidently the other direction. That’s alright.

Jesus never promised the broad road. He promised Himself. So tomorrow morning, before the headlines… Before social media… Before your growing to-do list…

Open the Scriptures.

Ask the Holy Spirit to remind you of what He has already written upon your heart (John 14:26). Honor your father and mother. Be quick to forgive. Stay generous. Stay humble. Walk quietly with Christ.

And when you feel like one small light in an increasingly dark world, remember this: The narrow gate has never been crowded. That’s not cause for discouragement. It’s cause for hope.

The Shepherd knows every sheep by name, and not one who belongs to Him is ever forgotten.
